seltz.title: World number ones: the ATP and WTA rankings through history
seltz.snippet:
The top spot in the men's and women's rankings is probably the most visible reference in professional tennis. Both systems are based on merit: the number one is the player who has accumulated the most points on tour over the previous 52 weeks. The ATP has used a computerised system since 23 August 1973, and since 1979 it has published an updated list every week. The WTA has done so since 3 November 1975.

The way points are counted has changed several times. Today the men's ranking adds up a player's best eighteen tournaments, with restrictions by category. Those counting events include the four Grand Slams, the eight mandatory Masters tournaments, the non-mandatory Masters 1000 event in Monte-Carlo, the best four ATP 500 events and the best two ATP 250 events. Players who qualify for the year-end ATP Finals add those points too, which can bring the total to nineteen tournaments. Between 1990 and 1999 the system counted a player's best fourteen results; from 2000 to 2008 it used the best eighteen; and from 2009 the ATP kept that approach but adopted a new point scale. A two-year window was used between August 2020 and August 2021 because of the pandemic, and the standard 52-week period returned afterwards. In 2024 tour-level point values were raised again.

In terms of weeks, the headline figure belongs to Novak Djokovic, with a record 428 weeks at world number one. Roger Federer holds the record for consecutive weeks at the top, 237. Djokovic also has the most year-end number one finishes, eight, including the two seasons affected by the pandemic. Pete Sampras finished six consecutive years at number one, and John McEnroe held the top spot a record fourteen times. Sampras and Djokovic are the only other players to have held it ten or more times, with eleven and ten stints respectively.

Before 1973, there was no official ranking system — writers, promoters, and national federations produced their own lists with no universal standard. The ATP, founded in 1972, introduced a computer ranking system based on tournament results weighted by prestige.

ultimate.snippet:
From [Novak Djokovic](https://www.atptour.com/en/players/novak-djokovic/d643/overview)'s record seven ATP Year-End No. 1 presented by Pepperstone finishes to [Roger Federer](https://www.atptour.com/en/players/roger-federer/f324/overview)'s 237 consecutive weeks at No. 1, several ATP Tour stars have smashed the record books at the top of the Pepperstone ATP Rankings.

[Novak Djokovic](https://www.atptour.com/en/players/novak-djokovic/d643/overview) made history on 6 November 2021 when he secured the year-end No. 1 presented by Pepperstone for a record seventh time, eclipsing the mark he previously shared with [Pete Sampras](https://www.atptour.com/en/players/pete-sampras/s402/overview). Djokovic, who ended the season atop of tennis’ mountain for the first time in 2011, lifted at least one major every year that he secured the year-end No. 1 (also 2011-12, '14-15, '18 and 20).

While Djokovic holds the ATP record of seven year-end No. 1 finishes, Sampras remains the only player in the history of the Pepperstone ATP Rankings to own six consecutive year-end No. 1 finishes.

While Djokovic has spent the most weeks at No. 1, Federer holds the record for the number of consecutive weeks in top spot with 237. The longest uninterrupted No. 1 reign in Pepperstone ATP Rankings history began on 2 February 2004, when Federer dethroned [Andy Roddick](https://www.atptour.com/en/players/andy-roddick/r485/overview) from No. 1 with his triumph at the [Australian Open](https://www.atptour.com/en/tournaments/australian-open/580/overview). He then embarked on an unprecedented period of dominance on the ATP Tour, remaining at No. 1 until 17 August 2008, when he was usurped by Nadal.
In the 237 consecutive weeks Federer spent at No. 1, he lifted 43 tour-level trophies, including 10 majors and three [Nitto ATP Finals](https://www.atptour.com/en/tournaments/nitto-atp-finals/605/overview) crowns.
